catalog_quote: 3.4 Stress While the segmental structure of basilectal Unserdeutsch shows an unambiguous substrate influence, the prosody shows the exact opposite influence of the lexifier language. The accent rules in Unserdeutsch are for the most part identical to those of Standard German. Word accent is usually morphologically conditioned, with accent falling on the first syllable of the root, which may be, but is not necessarily, the first syllable of the word. In certain cases, whether for morphological reasons or because the word is of non-German origin, this basic principle is not followed, and the accent is in a different position. When this is morphologically conditioned (such as with phrasal verbs), accent is in the same position as in Standard German. new_statements.quote: While the segmental structure of basilectal Unserdeutsch shows an unambiguous substrate influence, the prosody shows the exact opposite influence of the lexifier language. The accent rules in Unserdeutsch are for the most part identical to those of Standard German. Word accent is usually morphologically conditioned, with accent falling on the first syllable of the root, which may be, but is not necessarily, the first syllable of the word. [...] In words of non-German origin, accent follows the rules of the relevant source language. From a typological perspective, word accent in Unserdeutsch can therefore be considered free, as it can in principle fall on any syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress follows Standard German: it falls on the first syllable of the root (so usually word-initial in native Germanic vocabulary, but not when unstressed prefixes precede); morphologically conditioned exceptions (e.g. phrasal/particle verbs) pattern as in Standard German; loanwords keep the stress of their source language, so position is not phonologically fixed ('free'). Volker 1982: 28 concurs: stress is not phonemic; Germanic first-syllable pattern, even extended to some French loans (/káfe/ 'Kaffee', /íntesant/ 'interessant').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: Morphologically conditioned cases (e.g. phrasal verbs) stressed as in Standard German; words of non-German origin follow source-language stress. Volker 1982: 28 adds that some French loans are regularised to initial stress (/káfe/, /íntesant/) while /hɔspitál/ keeps French final stress and /optəmətríst/ takes final stress by the SG -ist rule. Meyer 2026: 37 notes no corpus-based study of stress exists yet.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent ('word accent'); description is of basilectal Unserdeutsch based on the Augsburg/Bern documentation corpus of elderly speakers now mostly in Australia. Sec. 3.3 adds that unstressed syllables have full [ɛ] rather than schwa and quantity contrasts are levelled, so stressed/unstressed syllable weight is near-symmetrical (syllable-language profile).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Unserdeutsch = Rabaul Creole German (unse1236, ISO uln), the German-lexifier creole of the Vunapope mission (East New Britain), speakers now mostly in Australia; the Maitz/Lindenfelser/Volker statement refers explicitly to basilectal Unserdeutsch (mesolectal/acrolectal speech is closer to Standard German). Volker 1982 is based on 1979-80 fieldwork with Vunapope speakers.

sources.note: p.28 'Stress': 'As in Standard German, stress is not phonemic in Rabaul Creole German. In general the language keeps to the Germanic stress pattern of always stressing the first syllable. In some cases Rabaul Creole German does this where Standard German does not: /káfe/ "coffee" (SG Kaffee), /íntesant/ "interesting" (SG interessant)'; /hɔspitál/ retains French final stress; /optəmətríst/ has final stress per the SG rule for -ist.

Manuscript chapter for Boas, Deumert, Louden & Maitz (eds.), Varieties of German Worldwide, Oxford University Press. 25 pp. Hosted on the Univ. Bern Unserdeutsch project literature page.
sources.note: Sec. 3.4 'Stress' (p.9): accent rules for the most part identical to Standard German; word accent morphologically conditioned, on the first syllable of the root (not necessarily first syllable of word); non-German-origin words follow the source language's stress; typologically 'free'. Sec. 3.3: basilectal UD is a syllable language, no vowel reduction in unstressed syllables, quantity contrast levelled.

sources.citation: Meyer, Lena. 2026. Sprachliche Variation in Unserdeutsch. Untersuchung einer bedrohten Kreolsprache (Empirische Linguistik 22). Berlin/Boston: De Gruyter. 342 pp. Open access CC-BY, DOI 10.1515/9783112223338.
sources.note: p.37 (sec. 3.3.1): 'Zur Betonung in Unserdeutsch liegen noch keine korpusbasierten Untersuchungen vor. Es wird allerdings angenommen, dass die Akzentmuster in Unserdeutsch ähnlich wie im Standarddeutschen funktionieren (Maitz et al. i. E.). Unserdeutsch hat einen Stammsilbenakzent, der wie im Standarddeutschen häufig auf die erste Silbe fällt.' Later chapters code Wortakzent/Fokusakzent as factors in consonant-cluster reduction.
